notes.front: In GitHub Actions, what is a workflow run, and what do its logs record?
notes.back: One run of a workflow; its logs include the status of each job and step.
notes.explanation: Every run of a workflow keeps its own logs, which you open from that workflow's list of runs in the Actions tab.
notes.example: Like one performance of a play: the script stays the same, but each night's show has its own record of what happened.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing workflow run history”
notes.evidence: You can view logs for each run of a workflow. Logs include the status for each job and step in a workflow.

notes.front: What is the visualization graph of a workflow run?
notes.back: A real-time graph, generated for every workflow run, that illustrates the run's progress.
notes.explanation: It shows each job with a status icon and draws lines between jobs for their dependencies, so you can monitor and debug the run.
notes.example: Like a live departure board at a station: each job is a train, and you see at a glance which have left, which are waiting and which depend on another.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using the visualization graph”
notes.evidence: Every workflow run generates a real-time graph that illustrates the run progress. You can use this graph to monitor and debug workflows.

notes.front: What is a workflow run log used for when a run fails?
notes.back: To view and search the build logs and diagnose the failure; you can also download logs and artifacts.
notes.explanation: Once you have found the cause in the log, you can re-run the workflow from the same page.
notes.example: Like a ship's logbook read after a storm: the entries tell you which watch first saw trouble.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”
notes.evidence: If the run failed, you can view and search the build logs to diagnose the failure and re-run the workflow. You can also view billable job execution minutes, or download logs and build artifacts.

notes.front: Besides the steps in your workflow file, which two steps does GitHub add to every job?
notes.back: "Set up job" and "Complete job".
notes.explanation: GitHub adds them to set up and to complete the job's execution, and logs them in the workflow run under those names.
notes.example: Like check-in and check-out on a hotel stay: you never booked them, but they bracket everything else you did.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Viewing logs to diagnose failures”
notes.evidence: In addition to the steps configured in the workflow file, GitHub adds two additional steps to each job to set up and complete the job's execution. These steps are logged in the workflow run with the names "Set up job" and "Complete job".

notes.front: What does step debug logging do?
notes.back: It increases the verbosity of a job's logs, during and after the job's execution.
notes.explanation: It is extra detail you switch on when the normal logs do not say enough, and it affects the job's logs both while it runs and afterwards.
notes.example: Like switching a car's dashboard from the simple display to the mechanic's view: the same journey, many more readings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling step debug logging”
notes.evidence: Step debug logging increases the verbosity of a job's logs during and after a job's execution.

notes.front: What does runner diagnostic logging add to a run's logs?
notes.back: Extra log files about how the runner is executing a job, added to the log archive.
notes.explanation: It looks at the runner rather than at your steps: two extra files go into the log archive.
notes.example: Like a flight recorder for the aircraft rather than the passenger list: it records how the machine did the work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling runner diagnostic logging”
notes.evidence: Runner diagnostic logging provides additional log files that contain information about how a runner is executing a job. Two extra log files are added to the log archive:

notes.front: In GitHub Actions, what can a re-run repeat?
notes.back: A whole workflow run, all its failed jobs, or specific jobs in it.
notes.explanation: You choose the scope: the entire run, just the jobs that failed, or the jobs you pick, within a time limit after the first run.
notes.example: Like reprinting a report: you can reprint all of it, only the pages that jammed, or one page you choose.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: You can re-run a workflow run, all failed jobs in a workflow run, or specific jobs in a workflow run up to 30 days after its initial run.

notes.front: What is a disabled workflow?
notes.back: A workflow stopped from being triggered while its file stays in the repository; you can re-enable it.
notes.explanation: Disabling stops the triggers without deleting the workflow file, and the workflow can easily be re-enabled on GitHub.
notes.example: Like switching a burglar alarm off at the panel while builders are in: the alarm stays fitted and can be switched back on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling and enabling a workflow”
notes.evidence: Disabling a workflow allows you to stop a workflow from being triggered without having to delete the file from the repo. You can easily re-enable the workflow again on GitHub.

notes.front: What access to a repository do you need to view its workflow run history?
notes.back: Read access.
notes.explanation: Opening the Actions tab, a workflow and its list of runs needs only read access to the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing workflow run history”
notes.evidence: Read access to the repository is required to perform these steps.

notes.front: What happens if `.github/workflows` contains an invalid workflow file?
notes.back: GitHub Actions generates a failed workflow run for every new commit.
notes.explanation: The docs therefore tell you to commit only valid workflow files to the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”
notes.evidence: Ensure that you only commit valid workflow files to your repository. If `.github/workflows` contains an invalid workflow file, GitHub Actions generates a failed workflow run for every new commit.

notes.front: When you open a failed job in a workflow run, which steps are expanded for you?
notes.back: Any failed steps, which are expanded automatically to show their results.
notes.explanation: The failing step's output is visible as soon as you open the job.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Viewing logs to diagnose failures”
notes.evidence: Any failed steps are automatically expanded to display the results.

notes.front: On GitHub-hosted runners, what does the "Set up job" step record?
notes.back: Details of the runner image, with a link to the list of preinstalled tools on the runner machine.
notes.explanation: It is where to look for the image and the preinstalled tools the job started with.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Viewing logs to diagnose failures”
notes.evidence: For jobs run on GitHub-hosted runners, "Set up job" records details of the runner image, and includes a link to the list of preinstalled tools that were present on the runner machine.

notes.front: You download the log archive of a run that was partially re-run. Which jobs does it contain?
notes.back: Only the jobs that were re-run.
notes.explanation: For a complete set of logs you must also download the archives of the earlier run attempts that ran the other jobs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Downloading logs”
notes.evidence: When you download the log archive for a workflow that was partially re-run, the archive only includes the jobs that were re-run. To get a complete set of logs for jobs that were run from a workflow, you must download the log archives for the previous run attempts that ran the other jobs.

notes.front: To enable step debug logging, set the secret or variable {{c1::`ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG`}} to `true` in the repository that contains the workflow.
notes.back: `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG`
notes.explanation: It is a setting in the repository that holds the workflow, not a line inside the workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling step debug logging”
notes.evidence: To enable step debug logging, set the following secret or variable in the repository that contains the workflow: `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` to `true`.

notes.front: To enable runner diagnostic logging, set the secret or variable {{c1::`ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG`}} to `true` in the repository that contains the workflow.
notes.back: `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG`
notes.explanation: Like step debug logging, it is switched on in the repository rather than in the workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling runner diagnostic logging”
notes.evidence: To enable runner diagnostic logging, set the following secret or variable in the repository that contains the workflow: `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG` to `true`.

notes.front: `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` is set both as a secret and as a variable, with different values. Which value is used?
notes.back: The secret's: it takes precedence over the variable.
notes.explanation: The docs state the same rule for `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG`, so a variable cannot override a secret for either setting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling step debug logging”
notes.evidence: If both the secret and variable are set, the value of the secret takes precedence over the variable.

notes.front: Which runner diagnostic log file holds information about coordinating and setting up runners to execute jobs?
notes.back: The runner process log.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two extra files that runner diagnostic logging adds to the log archive.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling runner diagnostic logging”
notes.evidence: The runner process log, which includes information about coordinating and setting up runners to execute jobs.

notes.front: Which runner diagnostic log file logs the execution of a job?
notes.back: The worker process log.
notes.explanation: It sits beside the runner process log in the downloaded log archive.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”, “Enabling runner diagnostic logging”
notes.evidence: The worker process log, which logs the execution of a job.

notes.front: Who can turn on runner diagnostic logging and step debug logging for a workflow re-run?
notes.back: Anyone who has access to run the workflow.
notes.explanation: It is an addition to setting the repository secret or variable, and applies to that re-run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”
notes.evidence: Additionally, anyone who has access to run a workflow can enable runner diagnostic logging and step debug logging for a workflow re-run.

notes.front: You can re-run a workflow run, its failed jobs or specific jobs up to {{c1::30 days}} after its initial run.
notes.back: 30 days
notes.explanation: The window counts from the run's initial run, whichever part of it you re-run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: You can re-run a workflow run, all failed jobs in a workflow run, or specific jobs in a workflow run up to 30 days after its initial run.

notes.front: Whose privileges does a re-run use?
notes.back: Those of the actor who first triggered the workflow, not those of the person who starts the re-run.
notes.explanation: Re-running someone else's run does not swap in your own privileges.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: Re-runs use the privileges of the actor who initially triggered the workflow, not the privileges of the actor who initiated the re-run.

notes.front: A re-run uses the same {{c1::`GITHUB_SHA`}} and `GITHUB_REF` as the original event that triggered the run.
notes.back: `GITHUB_SHA`
notes.explanation: The re-run repeats the original event's commit and Git ref.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: The workflow will also use the same `GITHUB_SHA` (commit SHA) and `GITHUB_REF` (git ref) of the original event that triggered the workflow run.

notes.front: A workflow run can be re-run at most {{c1::50}} times, counting both full re-runs and re-runs of some of its jobs.
notes.explanation: Re-running only a subset of jobs still counts towards the limit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: A workflow run can be re-run a maximum of 50 times. This limit includes both full re-runs and re-runs of a subset of jobs.

notes.front: Which `gh` command re-runs one specific job of a workflow run?
notes.back: `gh run rerun --job JOB_ID`, giving the ID of the job.
notes.explanation: You name the job by its own ID, not by the ID of the run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”, “Re-running a specific job in a workflow”
notes.evidence: To re-run a specific job in a workflow run, use the `run rerun` subcommand with the `--job` flag. Replace `JOB_ID` with the ID of the job that you want to re-run.

notes.front: Which `gh` command disables a workflow, and how can you name the workflow?
notes.back: `gh workflow disable`, naming the workflow by its name, ID or file name.
notes.explanation: If you leave the workflow out, `gh` offers an interactive menu to choose one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling and enabling a workflow”, “Disabling a workflow”
notes.evidence: To disable a workflow, use the `workflow disable` subcommand. Replace `workflow` with either the name, ID, or file name of the workflow you want to disable.

notes.front: When a public repository is forked, {{c1::scheduled}} workflows are disabled by default.
notes.back: scheduled
notes.explanation: This prevents unnecessary runs; in a public repository, scheduled workflows are also disabled automatically after 60 days without repository activity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling and enabling a workflow”
notes.evidence: To prevent unnecessary workflow runs, scheduled workflows may be disabled automatically. When a public repository is forked, scheduled workflows are disabled by default. In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.

notes.front: Which workflow runs can you delete, and what access does it take?
notes.back: Runs that have completed or are more than two weeks old; you need write access to the repository.
notes.explanation: Viewing runs needs only read access, but deleting one needs write access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deleting a workflow run”
notes.evidence: You can delete a workflow run that has been completed, or is more than two weeks old. Write access to the repository is required to perform these steps.

notes.front: What happens to a run's artifacts when the workflow run is deleted?
notes.back: They are deleted from storage along with it.
notes.explanation: Deleting the run removes every artifact associated with it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing workflow artifacts”, “Artifacts from deleted workflow runs”
notes.evidence: When a workflow run is deleted all artifacts associated with the run are also deleted from storage.

notes.front: By default, GitHub stores build logs and artifacts for {{c1::90}} days.
notes.explanation: You can download archived artifacts only before they expire, and the retention period can be customised depending on the type of repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Downloading workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: By default, GitHub stores build logs and artifacts for 90 days, and you can customize this retention period, depending on the type of repository.

notes.front: Can a deleted workflow artifact be restored?
notes.back: No: once you delete an artifact, it cannot be restored.
notes.explanation: Deleting an artifact also needs write access to the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing workflow artifacts”, “Deleting an artifact”
notes.evidence: Once you delete an artifact, it cannot be restored. Write access to the repository is required to perform these steps.

notes.front: Which value tells you the date an artifact is scheduled to be deleted?
notes.back: `expires_at`, a value returned for the artifact when you look it up through GitHub's programming interface.
notes.explanation: You can look the date up programmatically instead of working it out from the retention period.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Removing workflow artifacts”, “Finding the expiration date of an artifact”
notes.evidence: You can use the API to confirm the date that an artifact is scheduled to be deleted. For more information, see the `expires_at` value returned by the REST API.

notes.front: The endpoint for downloading an artifact returns a redirect link. How long is it valid, and in what format is the archive?
notes.back: One minute; the archive format must be `zip`.
notes.explanation: You find the link in the `Location:` header of the response.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions artifacts”, “Download an artifact”
notes.evidence: Gets a redirect URL to download an archive for a repository. This URL expires after 1 minute. Look for Location: in the response header to find the URL for the download. The :archive\_format must be zip.

notes.front: In a repository's list of cache entries, what three things can you see about each cache?
notes.back: How much disk space it uses, when it was created and when it was last used.
notes.explanation: You can also narrow the list by branch, or by cache key with `key: key-name` in the Filter caches field.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing caches”, “Viewing cache entries”
notes.evidence: In the cache list, you can see how much disk space each cache is using, when the cache was created, and when the cache was last used.

notes.front: A workflow never starts. What do the docs say to check first?
notes.back: That the workflow was not disabled manually: a disabled workflow does not respond to its triggers.
notes.explanation: Next, review the workflow's `on:` field to see what is expected to trigger it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Troubleshooting workflow triggers”
notes.evidence: First, make sure that your workflow wasn't disabled manually, see Disabling and enabling a workflow. A disabled workflow does not respond to its triggers. You can review your workflow's `on:` field to understand what is expected to trigger the workflow.

notes.front: Which two triggering events do the docs name as running only from the default branch?
notes.back: `issues` and `schedule`.
notes.explanation: Versions of the workflow file that exist outside the default branch will not trigger on these events.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Triggering event conditions”
notes.evidence: Some triggering events only run from the default branch (i.e. `issues`, `schedule`). Workflow file versions that exist outside of the default branch will not trigger on these events.

notes.front: Workflows will not run on `pull_request` activity if the pull request has a {{c1::merge conflict}}.
notes.back: merge conflict
notes.explanation: It is one of the triggering-event conditions to check when a pull request workflow does not start.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Triggering event conditions”
notes.evidence: Workflows will not run on `pull_request` activity if the pull request has a merge conflict.

notes.front: For path filtering, evaluating diffs is limited to the first {{c1::3,000}} files.
notes.explanation: If the changed files that match are not among those first files returned by the filter, the workflow will not run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Filtering and diff limits”
notes.evidence: For path filtering, evaluating diffs is limited to the first 3,000 files. If there are files changed that are not matched in the first 3,000 files returned by the filter, the workflow will not be run.

notes.front: Why might a scheduled workflow start late, and what reduces the chance?
notes.back: Scheduled events can be delayed at high load, such as the start of every hour; schedule it for a different time of the hour.
notes.explanation: If the load is high enough, some queued jobs may even be dropped.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Scheduled workflows running at unexpected times”
notes.evidence: Scheduled events can be delayed during periods of high loads of GitHub Actions workflow runs. High load times include the start of every hour. If the load is sufficiently high enough, some queued jobs may be dropped. To decrease the chance of delay, schedule your workflow to run at a different time of the hour.

notes.front: A job was skipped unexpectedly. Where in its log archive do you see how its `if` condition was evaluated?
notes.back: In `JOB-NAME/system.txt`, in the `Evaluating`, `Expanded` and `Result` lines.
notes.explanation: The `Expanded` line shows the runtime values substituted into the condition, which makes clear why it came out `true` or `false`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Debugging job conditions”
notes.evidence: Download the log archive from the job's menu. 3. Open the `JOB-NAME/system.txt` file. 4. Look for the `Evaluating`, `Expanded`, and `Result` lines. The `Expanded` line shows the actual runtime values that were substituted into your `if` condition

notes.front: Why do the docs recommend unique label names for larger and self-hosted runners?
notes.back: A label matching a preset label can cause assignment issues, with no guarantee which matching runner the job runs on.
notes.explanation: GitHub-hosted runners already use preset labels, so a clash leaves the choice of runner open.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Defining runner labels”
notes.evidence: We recommend using unique label names for larger and self-hosted runners. If a label matches to any of the existing preset labels, there can be runner assignment issues where there is no guarantee on which matching runner option the job will run on.

notes.front: A teammate with read access wants to know which step made last night's run fail. What should they do?
notes.choices:
A) Open the run from the workflow's list in the Actions tab and read the failed step's log
B) Ask an admin to turn on runner diagnostic logging and re-run it
C) Download the repository's artifacts and search them
D) Wait for write access, which the logs require
notes.back: A) Open the run from the workflow's list in the Actions tab and read the failed step's log
notes.choicesExplained: B: debug logging is for when the normal logs are not detailed enough; they may well be. C: artifacts are build outputs, not the step logs. D: viewing logs needs only read access.
notes.explanation: The run page shows which step caused the failure, and its build log is there to troubleshoot with read access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Viewing logs to diagnose failures”
notes.evidence: If your workflow run fails, you can see which step caused the failure and review the failed step's build logs to troubleshoot. You can see the time it took for each step to run.

notes.front: A job on a GitHub-hosted runner fails oddly, and you want to confirm which runner image and preinstalled tools it had. Which step's log do you open?
notes.choices:
A) "Complete job"
B) "Set up job"
C) The first step written in your workflow file
D) The last step written in your workflow file
notes.back: B) "Set up job"
notes.choicesExplained: A: "Complete job" finishes the job's execution; it does not record the image. C and D: your own steps log what they run, not the runner image.
notes.explanation: "Set up job" records the runner image and links to the list of preinstalled tools.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow run logs”, “Viewing logs to diagnose failures”
notes.evidence: For jobs run on GitHub-hosted runners, "Set up job" records details of the runner image, and includes a link to the list of preinstalled tools that were present on the runner machine.

notes.front: You suspect the runner itself went wrong while coordinating and setting up your job, and you want its own logs. What do you set to `true` in the repository?
notes.back: D) `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG`
notes.choicesExplained: A: step debug logging makes the job's own logs more verbose; it adds no runner log files. B: `runner.debug` is a context you read, not a setting you create. C: this is not a debug setting.
notes.explanation: `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG` adds the runner process log, which covers coordinating and setting up runners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enabling debug logging”
notes.evidence: To enable runner diagnostic logging, set the following secret or variable in the repository that contains the workflow: `ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG` to `true`.

notes.front: A workflow run failed 45 days ago, and you would like to repeat exactly that run. What can you do with the re-run feature?
notes.choices:
A) Re-run all its jobs, but not the failed jobs alone
B) Nothing: re-runs are possible only up to 30 days after the initial run
C) Re-run it once, as a final attempt
D) Re-run it with debug logging only
notes.back: B) Nothing: re-runs are possible only up to 30 days after the initial run
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: none of these is an exception; after 30 days no kind of re-run is offered for that run.
notes.explanation: The whole run, its failed jobs and specific jobs can each be re-run only within 30 days of the initial run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: You can re-run a workflow run, all failed jobs in a workflow run, or specific jobs in a workflow run up to 30 days after its initial run.

notes.front: A contributor's push triggered a run that failed. A maintainer with wider privileges re-runs it. Whose privileges does the re-run use?
notes.choices:
A) The contributor's, because they triggered the original run
B) Whichever of the two has fewer privileges
C) The maintainer's, because they started the re-run
D) The repository owner's
notes.back: A) The contributor's, because they triggered the original run
notes.choicesExplained: C: the person who starts the re-run does not lend their privileges. B and D: there is no comparison and no switch to the owner.
notes.explanation: Re-runs keep the privileges of the actor who initially triggered the workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”
notes.evidence: Re-runs use the privileges of the actor who initially triggered the workflow, not the privileges of the actor who initiated the re-run.

notes.front: Six jobs ran; four passed and two failed because a mirror was briefly down. You want the least repeated work. What do you choose?
notes.choices:
A) Re-run all jobs
B) Disable and re-enable the workflow
C) Re-run failed jobs
D) Delete the run and push again
notes.back: C) Re-run failed jobs
notes.choicesExplained: A: that repeats the four jobs that passed. B: disabling only stops triggers. D: deleting the run and pushing again starts every job afresh.
notes.explanation: Re-running failed jobs, in the web interface or with `gh run rerun --failed`, repeats only the jobs that failed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”, “Re-running failed jobs in a workflow”
notes.evidence: To re-run failed jobs in a workflow run, use the `run rerun` subcommand with the `--failed` flag.

notes.front: A matrix strategy created three jobs; only the Node 22 job failed. You want to repeat just that job, with debug logging, from a terminal. Which command?
notes.choices:
A) `gh run rerun --job JOB_ID --debug`
B) `gh run rerun RUN_ID --failed`
C) `gh run view --job JOB_ID --log`
D) `gh run rerun RUN_ID`
notes.back: A) `gh run rerun --job JOB_ID --debug`
notes.choicesExplained: D: that re-runs the whole failed run. B: that re-runs every failed job, which here happens to be one, but without debug logging. C: that only shows the log.
notes.explanation: Each matrix combination runs as its own job, so `--job` picks it and `--debug` enables runner diagnostic and step debug logging for the re-run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Re-running workflows and jobs”, “Re-running a specific job in a workflow”
notes.evidence: To re-run a specific job in a workflow run, use the `run rerun` subcommand with the `--job` flag. Replace `JOB_ID` with the ID of the job that you want to re-run. ```shell gh run rerun --job JOB_ID ``` To enable runner diagnostic logging and step debug logging for the re-run, use the `--debug` flag.

notes.front: A nightly workflow keeps calling a partner service that is down this week. You want it stopped now and back next week without editing any files. What do you do?
notes.choices:
A) Remove its `on:` key
B) Delete the workflow file
C) Cancel tonight's run only
D) Disable the workflow
notes.back: D) Disable the workflow
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: both change files in the repository. C: cancelling one run does not stop the next night's.
notes.explanation: Disabling stops the workflow being triggered without deleting its file, and it can easily be re-enabled.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling and enabling a workflow”
notes.evidence: Disabling a workflow allows you to stop a workflow from being triggered without having to delete the file from the repo. You can easily re-enable the workflow again on GitHub.

notes.front: A repository keeps the default retention settings. A colleague wants an artifact from a run four months ago. What is likely?
notes.choices:
A) It has expired, since logs and artifacts are kept for 90 days by default
B) It can be downloaded only with `gh`
C) It is still there, because artifacts never expire
D) It moved into the repository's releases
notes.back: A) It has expired, since logs and artifacts are kept for 90 days by default
notes.choicesExplained: C: artifacts do expire. B: `gh` downloads only artifacts that still exist. D: nothing moves artifacts into releases.
notes.explanation: Archived artifacts can be downloaded only before they expire, and the default period is 90 days.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Downloading workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: By default, GitHub stores build logs and artifacts for 90 days, and you can customize this retention period, depending on the type of repository.

notes.front: A script calls the artifact download endpoint, stores the redirect link, and fetches it five minutes later. The fetch fails. Why?
notes.choices:
A) The redirect link expires after one minute
B) The artifact was deleted by the call
C) The archive format must be `tar`
D) Download links work only in the web interface
notes.back: A) The redirect link expires after one minute
notes.choicesExplained: B: the endpoint returns a download link; it deletes nothing. C: the format must be `zip`. D: the endpoint exists so scripts can download artifacts.
notes.explanation: The link from the endpoint is short-lived, so the script should fetch it straight away.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions artifacts”, “Download an artifact”
notes.evidence: Gets a redirect URL to download an archive for a repository. This URL expires after 1 minute. Look for Location: in the response header to find the URL for the download. The :archive\_format must be zip.

notes.front: You add a workflow with `on: schedule` on a feature branch only. Days pass and it never runs. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Cron times follow your local time zone
B) Scheduled workflows need `workflow_dispatch` as well
C) `schedule` runs only from the default branch, and the file is not there
D) Scheduled runs are always disabled in private repositories
notes.back: C) `schedule` runs only from the default branch, and the file is not there
notes.choicesExplained: B: `schedule` needs no second trigger. A: the time zone would shift the run, not stop it. D: the docs disable scheduled workflows in forks of public repositories and after inactivity in public ones, not in every private repository.
notes.explanation: Workflow file versions outside the default branch do not trigger on `schedule`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Triggering event conditions”
notes.evidence: Some triggering events only run from the default branch (i.e. `issues`, `schedule`). Workflow file versions that exist outside of the default branch will not trigger on these events.

notes.front: Your team labels its own runner `ubuntu-latest`. Jobs with `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` sometimes land on it and sometimes elsewhere. What is the fix the docs point to?
notes.choices:
A) Add `max-parallel: 1`
B) Re-run the jobs with debug logging
C) Give the runner a unique label that does not match a preset label
D) Set `timeout-minutes`
notes.back: C) Give the runner a unique label that does not match a preset label
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: they limit parallel jobs and time, not runner choice. B: debug logging adds detail to the logs; it does not change which runner is chosen.
notes.explanation: A label matching a preset label gives no guarantee which matching runner the job runs on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Troubleshooting workflows”, “Defining runner labels”
notes.evidence: We recommend using unique label names for larger and self-hosted runners. If a label matches to any of the existing preset labels, there can be runner assignment issues where there is no guarantee on which matching runner option the job will run on.

notes.front: What is the difference between disabling a workflow and deleting its file?
notes.back: Disabling stops it being triggered but keeps the file, and is easily undone; deleting removes the file from the repository.
notes.explanation: Disabling is the way to stop triggers temporarily without touching the workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling and enabling a workflow”
notes.evidence: Disabling a workflow allows you to stop a workflow from being triggered without having to delete the file from the repo. You can easily re-enable the workflow again on GitHub.
